title: 2 Chronicles 9:13–28
context: 2 Chronicles 9:13–28 describes Solomon’s wealth: six hundred sixty-six talents of gold a year, golden shields, a great ivory throne overlaid with gold, gold drinking vessels, ships that went to Tarshish, tribute from the kings of the earth, horses and chariots, and silver as common as stones in Jerusalem. All the kings of the earth seek to hear the wisdom God had put in his heart. The parallel in 1 Kings 10:14–29 differs in some details, which these notes name without harmonizing: Kings gives the weight of the smaller shields as three minas where Chronicles gives three hundred shekels, and 9:25 gives four thousand stalls where 1 Kings 4:26 gives forty thousand. As the drafted notes on 1 Kings 10 observe, many readers notice the echo of Deuteronomy 17:16–17, which warns a king against multiplying horses, wives, and gold, though the text here does not comment. Both traditions read the passage as a description of the blessing God gave Solomon.

verses.text: Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was six hundred sixty-six talents of gold,
verses.arminianNotes: The gold that comes to Solomon in one year weighs six hundred sixty-six talents. Arminians see enormous wealth given by God, as promised in 2 Chronicles 1:12, and they note that 1 Kings 10:14 gives the same figure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the wealth as God’s blessing. Both traditions avoid attaching symbolic meaning to the number here, and they read it as a description of the riches of Solomon’s reign.

verses.text: in addition to that which the traders and merchants brought. All the kings of Arabia and the governors of the country brought gold and silver to Solomon.
verses.arminianNotes: Traders, merchants, the kings of Arabia, and governors also bring gold and silver. Arminian readers see wealth flowing into Jerusalem from many directions, a sign of Solomon’s influence among the nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as part of the picture of God’s blessing on Solomon. Both traditions note the parallel with 1 Kings 10:15 and treat the verse as shared ground.

verses.text: King Solomon made two hundred large shields of beaten gold. Six hundred shekels of beaten gold went to one large shield.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon makes two hundred large shields of beaten gold, each using six hundred shekels. A shekel weighed about 10 grams, a little over a third of an ounce. Arminians see the shields as a display of wealth and royal glory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the parallel with 1 Kings 10:16. Both traditions read the shields as ceremonial and recall that they were later taken by Shishak (2 Chronicles 12:9), a reminder that such glory did not last.

verses.text: He made three hundred shields of beaten gold. Three hundred shekels of gold went to one shield. The king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
verses.arminianNotes: He makes three hundred smaller shields with three hundred shekels each and puts them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon. Arminian readers note that 1 Kings 10:17 gives three minas for each shield, and they name the difference without resolving it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and leave the figures as they stand, consistent with the drafted notes on 1 Kings 10. Both traditions read the verse as part of the description of Solomon’s wealth.

verses.text: Moreover the king made a great throne of ivory, and overlaid it with pure gold.
verses.arminianNotes: The king makes a great ivory throne overlaid with pure gold. Arminians see the throne as a symbol of the splendor God gave Solomon’s reign, a visible sign of royal authority.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the parallel with 1 Kings 10:18. Both traditions read the verse as part of the Chronicler’s picture of a kingdom at the height of God’s blessing.

verses.text: There were six steps to the throne, with a footstool of gold, which were fastened to the throne, and armrests on either side by the place of the seat, and two lions standing beside the armrests.
verses.arminianNotes: The throne has six steps, a footstool of gold, armrests, and two lions beside them. Arminian readers note that 1 Kings 10:19 describes the throne’s round top rather than a footstool, and they name the difference without harmonizing it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and leave the descriptions as they stand. Both traditions read the details as showing the magnificence of Solomon’s throne without assigning symbolic meaning to them.

verses.text: Twelve lions stood there on the one side and on the other on the six steps. There was nothing like it made in any other kingdom.
verses.arminianNotes: Twelve lions stand on the six steps, and nothing like it was made in any other kingdom. Arminians see the throne’s uniqueness as reflecting the unique blessing God gave Solomon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as emphasizing the splendor of the kingdom. Both traditions note the parallel with 1 Kings 10:20 and avoid allegorizing the number of lions.

verses.text: All King Solomon’s drinking vessels were of gold, and all the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of pure gold. Silver was not considered valuable in the days of Solomon.
verses.arminianNotes: All Solomon’s drinking vessels and the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon are gold, and silver is not considered valuable. Arminian readers see the abundance of wealth as fulfilling God’s promise of riches to Solomon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as a description of extraordinary prosperity. Both traditions note the parallel with 1 Kings 10:21 and treat it as shared ground.

verses.text: For the king had ships that went to Tarshish with Huram’s servants. Once every three years, the ships of Tarshish came bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.
verses.arminianNotes: The king’s ships go to Tarshish with Huram’s servants and return every three years with gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks. Arminians note that 1 Kings 10:22 speaks of ships of Tarshish at sea, and they name the difference without resolving it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and leave the wording as it stands. Both traditions note that the identification of some of the animals is uncertain, and they read the verse as a picture of wide-ranging trade.

verses.text: So King Solomon exceeded all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon exceeds all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom. Arminian readers see the fulfillment of God’s promise in 2 Chronicles 1:12, which gave Solomon both wisdom and wealth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that this greatness was God’s gift. Both traditions note the parallel with 1 Kings 10:23 and read the verse as the summary of Solomon’s blessed reign.

verses.text: All the kings of the earth sought the presence of Solomon to hear his wisdom, which God had put in his heart.
verses.arminianNotes: All the kings of the earth seek Solomon’s presence to hear the wisdom God put in his heart. Arminians see the nations drawn to Israel through the wisdom God gave, a glimpse of God’s purpose to bless the nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that the wisdom came from God. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about God’s gifts bearing witness to the nations, consistent with 1 Kings 10:24.

verses.text: They each brought tribute: vessels of silver, vessels of gold, clothing, armor, spices, horses, and mules every year.
verses.arminianNotes: Each brings tribute every year: silver, gold, clothing, armor, spices, horses, and mules. Arminian readers see the nations honoring Solomon with their gifts, a sign of the peace and influence of his reign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as part of the picture of God’s blessing. Both traditions note the parallel with 1 Kings 10:25 and treat the verse as straightforward description.

verses.text: Solomon had four thousand stalls for horses and chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen that he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king at Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon has four thousand stalls for horses and chariots and twelve thousand horsemen. Arminians note that 1 Kings 4:26 gives forty thousand stalls and 1 Kings 10:26 gives fourteen hundred chariots, and they name the differences without resolving them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and leave the numbers as they stand. Both traditions note that many readers connect the horses with the warning in Deuteronomy 17:16, though the text here does not comment.

verses.text: He ruled over all the kings from the River even to the land of the Philistines, and to the border of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon rules over all the kings from the River to the land of the Philistines and the border of Egypt. Arminian readers see the extent of Solomon’s rule as fulfilling God’s promises about the land (compare Genesis 15:18).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note the parallel with 1 Kings 4:21. Both traditions read the verse as a high point in Israel’s history, while recognizing that the kingdom’s later division shows such greatness was not permanent.

verses.text: The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones, and he made cedars to be as abundant as the sycamore trees that are in the lowland.
verses.arminianNotes: The king makes silver as common as stones in Jerusalem and cedars as plentiful as sycamores. Arminians see vivid language describing extraordinary prosperity, as in 1 Kings 10:27.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as a picture of God’s blessing. Both traditions note that 2 Chronicles 1:15 uses similar words, and they read it as fulfillment of God’s promise of wealth.

verses.text: They brought horses for Solomon out of Egypt and out of all lands.
verses.arminianNotes: Horses are brought for Solomon from Egypt and from all lands. Arminian readers note that many connect this with Deuteronomy 17:16, which warns the king against multiplying horses or returning the people to Egypt for them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and name the echo by reference, as the drafted notes on 1 Kings 10 do. Both traditions note that the text does not comment here, and they do not supply the later account of 1 Kings 11.
